## Use PROCTOR from your coding agent (ADVISOR)[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#use-proctor-from-your-coding-agent-advisor)

This page is for developers whose coding agent runs [ADVISOR](https://github.com/waynestate/advisor), the stack's read-only MCP server. PROCTOR ships an ADVISOR module, so the agent can ask PROCTOR two questions without leaving its sandbox: "which rules do you check, and which ones block a deploy?" and "what do you say about this app right now?" Both answers come from PROCTOR's own classes. Next, see [Checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html) for every check in prose and [Deploy gate](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html) for the deploy-time rule set.

### Install ADVISOR[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#install-advisor)

In the app, install ADVISOR as a dev dependency:

```bash
composer require --dev waynestate/advisor
```

Then add one line to the app's `modules.json` (or point `ADVISOR_MODULES_FILE` at a file that holds it):

```json
{
    "modules": [
        "Waynestate\\Proctor\\Advisor\\ProctorModule"
    ]
}
```

PROCTOR does not require ADVISOR, and ADVISOR does not require PROCTOR: the module only loads when both are installed and `modules.json` names it.

### The two read-only tools[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#the-two-read-only-tools)

Both tools run in-process: no subprocess, no network, nothing written, and neither reads `.env`. `proctor_rules` takes no arguments. `proctor_check` takes exactly one, `path`: the app folder, inside the project root (default: the root itself). A path outside the root, or one that is not a folder, is refused.

#### proctor_rules[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#proctor-rules)

`proctor_rules` lists every check PROCTOR registers, in the order a report prints them, straight from `CheckSet`. It returns `proctor_version` and `rules`, one entry per check:

- `id`: the check id, for example `php-floor`.
- `rule_id`: its rule id, `proctor/<id>`. A check may report named rules under it (`proctor/<id>/<rule>`); the [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html) page lists them all.
- `in_gate`: `true` when `proctor gate` runs the check at deploy time.
- `docs`: the docs page that explains it.

One rule, as it comes back:

```json
{
    "id": "lock-committed",
    "rule_id": "proctor/lock-committed",
    "in_gate": true,
    "docs": "https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#lock-committed"
}
```

#### proctor_check[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#proctor-check)

`proctor_check` runs PROCTOR's checks on the app folder with PROCTOR's own `CheckRunner`, the way `proctor check` runs them by default: the CREED policy PROCTOR bundles, today's date and the app's `policy-overrides.json` when it has one. It returns:

- `findings`: each with `rule_id`, `status` (`pass`, `info`, `warning` or `fail`), `message`, `file` and `line` (`null` when the finding is about the app as a whole). Overrides are already applied, as in a report.
- `counts`: the number of findings per status.
- `verdict`: `fail` when any finding fails, else `pass`.
- `skipped`: the checks it left out, each with `id` and `reason` (see below).
- `ran`, `app` and `source`: what ran, on which folder (relative to the root), against which policy and for which date.

A missing or malformed `composer.json` or `policy-overrides.json` comes back as a tool error with PROCTOR's own message, the same one `proctor check` prints before it exits 2.

### What is skipped, and why[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#what-is-skipped-and-why)

Some checks cannot run inside ADVISOR's sandbox, so `proctor_check` leaves them out and lists them under `skipped`:

| Check | Reason | What it would run |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `composer-audit` | `starts a subprocess` | `composer audit` |
| `composer-version` | `starts a subprocess` | `composer --version` |
| `instant-client-committed` | `starts a subprocess` | git, to see what is committed |
| `wayneui-forked-views` | `starts a subprocess` | `git ls-files` |
| `wayneui-outdated` | `starts a subprocess` | `composer show` (which asks Packagist) and git |
| `node-eol`, `env-outside-config`, `raw-identity-header`, `served-folder`, `world-writable` | `starts a subprocess` | `git ls-files`, to grade only committed files |
| `app-key` | `reads .env` | reads committed env files for an `APP_KEY` |

`mysql-eol` does run: it reads `.env.example` and `.env.squire.example`, the committed placeholder files, never `.env`. An override in `policy-overrides.json` for a skipped check is not reported as unused, since its check did not run.

So a `pass` from `proctor_check` is a partial pass. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` for every check, or ADVISOR's own `run_proctor_check` tool, which starts PROCTOR as a subprocess under ADVISOR's allowlist.

Note

The agent reports; PROCTOR decides. Every answer names its source and says plainly what ran and what did not, and the run in CI is the one that passes or fails a build. A practice paper is a fine way to study, but it is not the exam.

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/advisor.html#related)

- [Checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html)
- [Deploy gate](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html)
- [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html)
- [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)

---

Source: https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html

## App checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#app-checks)

This page covers the seven PROCTOR checks that read the app's own files rather than its Composer metadata: the Node line it builds on, the MySQL or MariaDB image it runs, `env()` calls outside config, identity headers read directly, a committed APP_KEY, files a stranger can download from `public/`, and `chmod 777`. Each one holds a CREED practice. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` against the app path and fix what the report names. The proctor walks the aisles as well as reading the papers.

`node-eol` can fail a run. The other six warn, never fail: `mysql-eol` warns until Citadel's shared database server offers a supported MySQL (D-008), and a new check must not turn a passing app into a failing one.

### node-eol[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#node-eol)

`node-eol` grades every Node version the repository pins against the policy's `node` lines as of `--today`. The sources:

- `.nvmrc` and `.node-version` (the first line that is not a comment);
- package.json `volta.node`;
- an official `node` image in `.gitlab-ci.yml`, on an `image:` or `name:` line (`node:22`, `node:24-alpine`, `docker.io/library/node:22`, or one behind a registry host or a `$CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_...` prefix);
- an official `node` image on a `FROM` line in a `Dockerfile`, `Containerfile`, `Dockerfile.*` or `*.Dockerfile`.

Each source gets the same table as `php-floor`:

| State | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Active | pass, naming the active end date |
| Security only | warning, naming the security end date and the days left |
| End of life | fail, naming the security end date |
| Past the security end date plus the grace window | fail as `eol_grace_expired` |

An active override downgrades the eol fail to a warning, never the grace-expired one.

package.json `engines.node` is a declaration, not what runs, so its lowest allowed major is graded the same way but warns at worst (`proctor/node-eol/engines`). An odd major (21, 23, 25) is never an LTS line and never a target, so it warns wherever it is named (`proctor/node-eol/odd-major`).

No finding when the policy has no node component, when the repository names no Node version, for aliases (`lts/*`, `node`, `latest`), for image tags without a version (`node:lts-alpine`), and for another organization's image that happens to be called node (`someorg/node:14`).

Fix by moving the pin to an active even line, in every place the report names: the `.nvmrc`, the CI image and the Dockerfile should agree.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `node-eol` | `proctor/node-eol` |
| `node-eol` | `proctor/node-eol/engines` |
| `node-eol` | `proctor/node-eol/odd-major` |

### mysql-eol[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#mysql-eol)

`mysql-eol` grades every MySQL or MariaDB version the repository names against the policy's `mysql` and `mariadb` lines as of `--today`. The sources:

- an official `mysql` or `mariadb` image on an `image:` line in a root `docker-compose*.yml` or `compose*.yml` (`mysql:8.0`, `mariadb:10.11`, `docker.io/library/mysql:8.4`, or one behind a registry host or a `$VAR` prefix);
- `SQUIRE_MYSQL_IMAGE=mysql:<version>` in `.env.squire.example` or `.env.example`.

A `@sha256:` digest after the tag is tolerated: the version still comes from the tag. Each source gets the same table as `php-floor`, except an active version stays silent instead of passing:

| State | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Active | silent |
| Security only | warning, naming the security end date and the days left |
| End of life | warning, naming the security end date |
| Past the security end date plus the grace window | warning as `eol_grace_expired` |

Every row warns, never fails, until Citadel offers a supported MySQL (D-008). No override is needed while that holds: every graded state already warns.

No finding when the policy has no `mysql` or `mariadb` component, when the repository names no database version, or for another organization's image that happens to be called mysql (`someorg/mysql:8.0`). A bare major tag such as `mysql:8` is a floating tag and gets a warning to pin a major.minor; it is not graded as a guessed line.

Fix by moving the image to an active line, in every place the report names: the compose file and the env example should agree.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `mysql-eol` | `proctor/mysql-eol` |

### env-outside-config[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#env-outside-config)

`env-outside-config` warns for every `env()` call in a Laravel app outside its config files. After `php artisan config:cache`, Laravel no longer loads .env, so the call returns null in production while it works on a laptop.

It runs only on a Laravel app: an `artisan` file at the root, or `laravel/framework` in composer.json `require`. It scans every `*.php` file except the top-level `config/` and `bootstrap/cache/`, and skips `tests/`, `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `storage/` and `.git/` at any depth.

PHP is read on the syntax tree with names resolved, so `env()` in a comment or a string, a method named `env` (`$app->env()`) and a function imported from another namespace under the name `env` are not flagged. A Blade template is matched line by line and only with a quoted first argument (`{{ env('APP_NAME') }}`); Blade's own `@env('local')` directive is not a call.

Larastan enforces the same rule, so a call that carries its ignore marker for it (`@phpstan-ignore larastan.noEnvCallsOutsideOfConfig`, on the same line or on a comment line right above) was reviewed already. It is an info note (`proctor/env-outside-config/suppressed`), visible in the report but not counted. A closure in `bootstrap/app.php` that runs before config is loaded is the usual reason.

Fix by reading the variable in a config file (`'url' => env('APP_URL')` in `config/app.php`) and calling `config('app.url')` where it is used.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `env-outside-config` | `proctor/env-outside-config` |
| `env-outside-config` | `proctor/env-outside-config/suppressed` |

### raw-identity-header[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#raw-identity-header)

`raw-identity-header` warns, never fails, when app code reads an identity header directly instead of taking the user from SESAME. Drawbridge, the gateway, signs the session into the `X-Sesame-Assertion` header and passes the user's claims as request headers (`REMOTE_USER`, `X-Authenticated-*`, `X-Drawbridge-*`, `OIDC_CLAIM_*`); only SESAME's gateway driver may open that pair, because it verifies the signature before a claim becomes the logged-in user (CREED auth-3). App code that reads the assertion or a claim header itself accepts whatever value the proxy, or a client, put there.

It runs on every app and scans every `*.php` file except `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `storage/`, `tests/` and `.git/` at any depth.

PHP is read on the syntax tree with names resolved, so a header name in a comment or a log string, a variable named `$REMOTE_USER`, and `getenv()` with a computed argument are not flagged. Flagged read positions: a string key on `$_SERVER` or `$_ENV`, the quoted argument of `getenv()` or `apache_getenv()`, the quoted first argument of a method named `header`, `server`, `hasHeader`, `getHeader` or `getHeaderLine` (and of `get()` on a `->headers` object), and a string key on the result of `getallheaders()` or `apache_request_headers()`, directly or through a variable assigned from them.

Names match case-insensitively with `-` and `_` interchangeable. Where the read comes from `$_SERVER` or the environment (and from `request()->server()`, which reads the same bag) the `HTTP_` prefix Apache adds to request headers is accepted too. `X-Sesame-Assertion` is the signed assertion itself, so it is flagged like any other direct read; `PHP_AUTH_USER` is basic-auth material, so it is not an identity claim and is not flagged. A file that does not parse is skipped here; the portability check reports it.

Blade templates (`*.blade.php`) are not PHP until compiled, so a Blade line is matched with a pattern for `$_SERVER['...']` and `request()->header('...')` / `request()->server('...')`.

Fix by taking the user from SESAME (the gateway driver) and reading the claims it returns.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `raw-identity-header` | `proctor/raw-identity-header` |

### app-key[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#app-key)

`app-key` warns when the repository gives away the Laravel APP_KEY, or makes a leaked one worse. Whoever holds the key can forge encrypted payloads the app will unserialize, which can mean code execution.

| Rule id | Warns when |
| --- | --- |
| `proctor/app-key/committed-env` | A real env file is committed: `.env`, `.env.production`, or any `.env.*` that is not an example or a test file. |
| `proctor/app-key/committed-key` | A committed env file, examples included, sets `APP_KEY` or `APP_PREVIOUS_KEYS` to a real key (`base64:` and 16 or 32 bytes), or `config/app.php` carries one as a literal. The key is never printed. |
| `proctor/app-key/cookie-sessions` | `SESSION_DRIVER=cookie` in a committed env file, or a `cookie` default in `config/session.php`: every session is sealed with the APP_KEY, so a leaked key opens all of them. |

A real env file is graded only when PROCTOR knows it is committed: git lists it, or `CI`, `GITLAB_CI` or `GITHUB_ACTIONS` is set, where the checkout holds only what the repository holds. A developer's own `.env` on a laptop never raises a flag. Example files (`.example`, `.dist`, `.sample`, `.template`) are always graded; test files (`.env.testing`, `.env.test`, `.env.ci`, `.env.dusk.*`) are skipped.

Fix by running `git rm --cached` on the file, adding it to .gitignore and committing a `.env.example` with placeholders. Then rotate the key with `php artisan key:generate` on every environment that used it, and every other secret the file held. Move sessions to the `database` or `redis` driver.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `app-key` | `proctor/app-key` |
| `app-key` | `proctor/app-key/committed-env` |
| `app-key` | `proctor/app-key/committed-key` |
| `app-key` | `proctor/app-key/cookie-sessions` |

### served-folder[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#served-folder)

`served-folder` warns when a committed file under the top-level `public/` is something a stranger should not be able to download:

- a PHP file that calls `phpinfo()`, which shows the server configuration and environment (`proctor/served-folder/phpinfo`);
- a database dump (`*.sql`, `*.sql.gz`, `*.sql.zip`, `*.sql.bz2`, `*.dump`), a backup or editor copy (`*.bak`, `*.backup`, `*.old`, `*.orig`, `*.swp`, `*.swo`, a name ending in `~`), a log, an env file, or a database admin tool (`adminer*.php`) (`proctor/served-folder/debug-file`).

No finding when the app has no `public/` folder. Fix by deleting the file, or moving it out of `public/` and out of the repository.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `served-folder` | `proctor/served-folder` |
| `served-folder` | `proctor/served-folder/debug-file` |
| `served-folder` | `proctor/served-folder/phpinfo` |

### crlf-deploy-script[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#crlf-deploy-script)

`crlf-deploy-script` fails when a deploy script has Windows line endings (CRLF): bash on Linux reads the carriage return as part of each command, so `set -e` becomes `set -e\r` and the script breaks on the host that runs it.

Scanned: the top-level `build.sh` and `release.sh`, and every `.sh` file under a `deployments/`, `deploy_scripts/`, `deploy/` or `scripts/` directory at any depth. Skipped at any depth: `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `.git/`. One finding per file, on the line of its first carriage return.

Fix by converting the file to LF (`sed -i 's/\r$//' build.sh`, or the editor's line-ending setting) and adding `*.sh text eol=lf` to .gitattributes, so Git keeps it LF on every machine.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `crlf-deploy-script` | `proctor/crlf-deploy-script` |

### world-writable[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html#world-writable)

`world-writable` warns when the repository sets mode 777, which lets any process on the host change the file or folder:

- `chmod` with `777`, `0777`, `a+rwx` or `ugo+rwx` (flags such as `-R` allowed) in a shell script, a `Dockerfile` or `Containerfile`, a `Makefile`, `.gitlab-ci.yml`, or the `scripts` of composer.json and package.json;
- a PHP `chmod()` call whose mode is the literal `0777`.

Comment lines, the sticky `1777` and `mkdir()` (the umask still applies to it) are not flagged; `tests/` is skipped.

Fix by giving the web server user write access to the folders it needs (`storage/` and `bootstrap/cache/` in Laravel) and nothing more. Whether the container runs as a non-root user is a runtime fact, outside what PROCTOR reads.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `world-writable` | `proctor/world-writable` |

- [PHP checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html)

## CI checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#ci-checks)

This page covers the PROCTOR checks that verify CI pipelines run `composer ci`, that Preflight includes are pinned, and that deploy scripts and committed files keep the app portable. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` against the app path, then fix the finding the report names. PROCTOR watches the exam and does not hand out answers.

### ci-pipelines[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#ci-pipelines)

`ci-pipelines` enforces the CI contract. For a stack package (a composer.json `name` starting with `waynestate/`), both `.gitlab-ci.yml` and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` must exist and run `composer ci`; a missing or incomplete file is a failure. For any other project, a missing or incomplete `.gitlab-ci.yml` is a warning and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is optional.

The files are parsed as YAML, not grepped: a `composer ci` that only appears in a comment is not a script line, and a GitLab job is a top-level map with a `script` key. A GitHub job counts when a step runs `composer ci` or calls a reusable workflow with `ci-command: composer ci`.

A private stack package that sets `extra.proctor.github-mirror` to `false` in composer.json must never be on GitHub: a missing `.github/workflows/ci.yml` then gives no finding, and a present one warns (`proctor/ci-pipelines/github-private`) along with the warning-only rules.

Two more rules warn, and never fail, for stack packages and other projects alike:

- A GitHub `uses:` ref that is not a 40-hex commit SHA (`proctor/ci-pipelines/unpinned-uses`).
- A pipeline environment that switches Composer's audit or blocking policy off (`proctor/ci-pipelines/composer-audit-off`): `COMPOSER_NO_AUDIT` or `COMPOSER_NO_BLOCKING` set to anything but an empty string, `0` or `false`, or `COMPOSER_AUDIT_ABANDONED` set to `ignore`. On GitLab these come from the top-level or job `variables:` (a scalar or a map with a `value` key); on GitHub from the top-level, job or step `env:`.

When nothing needs fixing the check passes with `both pipelines run composer ci`, or `gitlab pipeline runs composer ci` when there is no GitHub workflow.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/gitlab-missing` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/gitlab-parse` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/gitlab-no-ci` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/github-missing` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/github-parse` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/github-no-ci` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/github-private` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/unpinned-uses` |
| `ci-pipelines` | `proctor/ci-pipelines/composer-audit-off` |

Fix a failing pipeline by adding a GitLab job whose `script` runs `composer ci`, adding a GitHub workflow that runs `composer ci` or calls a reusable workflow with `ci-command: composer ci`, and pinning every `uses:` ref to a commit SHA.

### preflight-pinned[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#preflight-pinned)

`preflight-pinned` warns, and never fails, when an app includes a Preflight component at a moving ref or re-declares what an included Preflight job runs. A Preflight include is an `include:` entry whose `component:` path contains `/preflight/`.

- When the ref after the last `@` is neither a full release tag (`MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH` such as `0.3.0`, optional leading `v`) nor a 40-lowercase-hex commit SHA it warns (`proctor/preflight-pinned/unpinned`). A branch such as `main`, `~latest`, a partial version such as `0.3` or `1` (GitLab resolves it to the newest matching release), or no `@` at all all count as moving. Pin a release tag such as `@0.3.0` or a commit SHA; published stack tags are never moved or deleted, so a release tag is a pin (D-054).
- When the app declares one of the Preflight job names (`proctor`, `php-test`, `composer-audit`, `sbom`, `pint`, `phpstan`, `eslint`, `renovate`, `package-publish`) with `script`, `before_script` or `after_script` while a Preflight component is included, it warns (`proctor/preflight-pinned/script-override`).

With nothing to flag it passes: `Preflight includes are pinned`, or `no Preflight components included` when there is no pipeline, a parse error or no Preflight include.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `preflight-pinned` | `proctor/preflight-pinned` |
| `preflight-pinned` | `proctor/preflight-pinned/unpinned` |
| `preflight-pinned` | `proctor/preflight-pinned/script-override` |

### portability[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#portability)

`portability` warns when code hard-codes a platform fact: an absolute host path, a hard-coded proxy address, a local-disk session store, or a `php_value`/`php_flag` line in `.htaccess`.

PHP files are matched on the syntax tree (nikic/php-parser with names resolved), not with regular expressions, so a comment or string that merely mentions a banned call is not flagged, and a call split over several lines, or hidden behind a `use function ... as ...` alias, is. A call through a variable (`$f()`) is reported as an info note, never as a pass.

Scanned: every `*.php` file, every file under the top-level `config/` directory, and every `.htaccess`. Skipped at any depth: `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `storage/`, `tests/` and `.git/`; in a Laravel app (an `artisan` file at the project root) also the top-level `bootstrap/cache/`, which holds the generated output of `php artisan optimize` (`config.php`, `routes-v7.php`, `services.php`, `packages.php`, `events.php`) instead of app code. A raw-PHP app that keeps its own `bootstrap/cache/` folder is scanned as before.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/host-path` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/proxy-address` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/local-session` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/htaccess-php-setting` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/parse-error` |
| `portability` | `proctor/portability/dynamic-call` |

### destructive-deploy[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#destructive-deploy)

`destructive-deploy` fails when a deploy script runs an artisan command that drops or rebuilds the database (`migrate:fresh`, `migrate:refresh`, `migrate:reset`, `db:wipe`), which erases production data on every deploy.

Danger

A drop-and-rebuild command in a deploy script wipes the live database on every release. Replace it with a plain migration.

It scans `.sh` and `.php` files under a top-level `deployments/`, `deploy_scripts/`, `deploy/` or `scripts/` directory, the top-level `build.sh`, `release.sh` and `.gitlab-ci.yml`, and the `scripts` section of composer.json. Shell comments are ignored.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `destructive-deploy` | `proctor/destructive-deploy` |

Fix by running plain `php artisan migrate --force` in the deploy.

### instant-client-committed[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#instant-client-committed)

`instant-client-committed` warns when Oracle Instant Client is committed to the repo: an `instantclient*.zip` or `instantclient*.rpm` archive, any file under a directory named `instantclient` or `instantclient_*` (an unzipped install), or a loose client library such as `libclntsh.so`, `libociei.so` or `oci.dll`.

Only committed files count: the git-tracked files when the app path sits in a git repository and git can be run, otherwise the files on disk. Skipped at any depth: `vendor/`, `node_modules/` and `.git/`. One warning per match: the archive, the topmost matching directory, or the loose file, each reported with its total size in MB.

Note

This is a warning, not a failure: Citadel's images already include Instant Client, and the WSU Sail and Docker images will too.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `instant-client-committed` | `proctor/instant-client-committed` |

Fix by deleting it, running `git rm -r --cached` on the path PROCTOR reports, and adding that path to `.gitignore`.

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html#related)

- [WayneUI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html)
- [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)

---

Source: https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html

## Composer checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#composer-checks)

This page covers the six PROCTOR checks that read composer.json and composer.lock: unbounded constraints, unsafe composer settings, the committed lock, audit results, the Composer version on PATH, and credentials in repository URLs. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` against the app path, then fix the finding the report names. The proctor checks the pens before it checks the answers.

### unbounded-constraints[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#unbounded-constraints)

`unbounded-constraints` fails for every runtime constraint that is `*`, names a `dev-` branch, carries `@dev`, has a lower bound with no upper bound, or matches the policy's `banned_constraints`. Each unbounded constraint is its own failure (`proctor/unbounded-constraints/unbounded`), naming the package and the offending constraint.

Three more rules warn, and never fail:

- A `path` or `vcs` repository (`proctor/unbounded-constraints/repository`).
- A `minimum-stability` below stable (`proctor/unbounded-constraints/minimum-stability`).
- A repository URL that is plain http (`proctor/unbounded-constraints/insecure-url`).

`require-dev`, `php`, `ext-*` and `lib-*` are not checked. With nothing to flag it passes: `all require constraints are bounded`. No open-ended answers in this hall.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `unbounded-constraints` | `proctor/unbounded-constraints` |
| `unbounded-constraints` | `proctor/unbounded-constraints/unbounded` |
| `unbounded-constraints` | `proctor/unbounded-constraints/repository` |
| `unbounded-constraints` | `proctor/unbounded-constraints/minimum-stability` |
| `unbounded-constraints` | `proctor/unbounded-constraints/insecure-url` |

### composer-config[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#composer-config)

`composer-config` warns when the `config` block of composer.json opens a door Composer closes by default:

- `allow-plugins` set to `true`: any plugin may run code during install (`proctor/composer-config/allow-plugins-all`).
- `secure-http` set to `false`: Composer may use plain HTTP for repositories (`proctor/composer-config/secure-http-off`).
- `lock` set to `false`: composer.json can change without a new lock (`proctor/composer-config/lock-off`).
- `audit.block-insecure` set to `false`: insecure versions are not blocked (`proctor/composer-config/audit-blocking-off`).
- `config.policy` set to `false`: Composer enforces no dependency policy (`proctor/composer-config/policy-off`).
- `policy.malware` set to `false`: malware results are not enforced (`proctor/composer-config/policy-malware-off`).
- `policy.advisories` set to `false`: advisories are not enforced (`proctor/composer-config/policy-advisories-off`).

It notes, as an info finding, when `require.php` is set without `config.platform.php` (`proctor/composer-config/platform-php-unset`): the lock then resolves against the local PHP. Warning and info only, never a fail, so an app that passes today keeps passing. With nothing to flag it passes: `no unsafe values in the composer config block`.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/allow-plugins-all` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/secure-http-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/lock-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/audit-blocking-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/policy-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/policy-malware-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/policy-advisories-off` |
| `composer-config` | `proctor/composer-config/platform-php-unset` |

### lock-committed[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#lock-committed)

`lock-committed` fails when composer.lock is missing from the app path. When the lock is present and its `content-hash` is a real 32-hex hash, it warns (`proctor/lock-committed/out-of-sync`) when the hash no longer matches composer.json, so a stale lock that still installs is visible instead of silent; the warning never changes the exit code.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `lock-committed` | `proctor/lock-committed` |
| `lock-committed` | `proctor/lock-committed/out-of-sync` |

### composer-audit[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#composer-audit)

`composer-audit` runs `composer audit --format=json --locked --no-plugins --no-interaction --abandoned=<policy>` against the app path and grades the result:

- Advisories at or above the policy's `audit_severity_threshold` fail; lower ones warn (`proctor/composer-audit/advisory`). Each finding names the package, the version locked in composer.lock, the advisory's CVE (or its advisory id when there is no CVE), its title and its severity.
- An advisory on a package that composer.lock lists only in `packages-dev` is a warning at any severity, with the message ending in ` [dev dependency]` after the severity in parentheses. A name in both the `packages` and `packages-dev` lists counts as runtime, and a name the lock does not list at all is graded as runtime too.
- An advisory the app ignores in its own composer.json (`config.policy.advisories.ignore-id`, `config.policy.advisories.ignore`, or the legacy `config.audit.ignore`) is a warning, not a fail, and so is anything composer has already moved to its ignored section.
- Abandoned packages follow the policy's `abandoned_packages` rule (`proctor/composer-audit/abandoned`), the same value CI's own `composer audit` reads, and PROCTOR passes it to the audit as `--abandoned`. Under `fail` (the bundled policy's value, and the default when a policy does not carry the rule) each abandoned package is a fail; under `report` it is a warning; under `ignore` it is not reported. The message names the replacement when the package's author suggested one (`vendor/pkg is abandoned; use replacement/pkg instead`) and says so when there is none (`vendor/pkg is abandoned with no named replacement`). An abandoned package the app ignores in its own composer.json (`config.policy.abandoned.ignore`, or the legacy `config.audit.ignore-abandoned` while there is no `config.policy.abandoned` block) is a warning, not a fail, the same as an ignored advisory, and a `composer-audit` override whose `package` field matches it downgrades the fail too ([Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)). Composer exits 1 for an abandoned package under `fail`, so that exit is explained by the list and does not earn the exit-code fail below. A proctor marks the empty desk absent, whatever excuse the note on it gives.
- When the composer executable is not on PATH or the app has no composer.lock, the check fails with a message that starts with `not audited:` (`proctor/composer-audit/skipped`), because a green run that audited nothing is worse than a red one. Install Composer, commit the lock, or record an active `composer-audit` override in policy-overrides.json with a reason and an expiry to downgrade the fail to a warning ([Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)).

When the audit runs but its stdout is not parseable JSON, the check fails (`proctor/composer-audit/could-not-run`) with a message that starts with `not audited:` and carries the first stderr line, because a green run that audited nothing is worse than a red one. Since Composer 2.10 the audit exits 1 when anything failed it, so a non-zero exit whose JSON lists nothing PROCTOR can read (a malware or policy block, or an error) is itself a fail (`proctor/composer-audit/exit-code`), and only a clean exit with a clean result passes.

A package pattern in `config.policy.advisories.ignore` may use `*`, matched the way composer does, case-insensitively. A warning (`proctor/composer-audit/ignore-entries`) reports the number of ignore entries in composer.json: `config.policy.advisories.ignore-id`, `config.policy.advisories.ignore`, `config.policy.advisories.ignore-severity`, `config.policy.abandoned.ignore`, or the legacy `config.audit.ignore`, `config.audit.ignore-severity` and `config.audit.ignore-abandoned` (the two legacy fallbacks count only while their matching `config.policy` block is absent), so they move to the dated override file ([Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)). An ignore entry that no active `composer-audit` override in policy-overrides.json backs is a fail of its own (`proctor/composer-audit/unbacked-ignore`), because an ignore without a dated approval never expires: an override backs the entry when its `advisory` field equals the entry's advisory id case-insensitively, its `package` field matches the entry's package the way composer matches patterns, or it carries no scope at all, and an entry that names neither an id nor a package (an ignore-severity level) is backed by an unscoped override only. The proctor checks the invigilator's mark against its own answer sheet, and refuses to sign a green for a red pen.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/advisory` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/abandoned` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/skipped` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/could-not-run` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/exit-code` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/ignore-entries` |
| `composer-audit` | `proctor/composer-audit/unbacked-ignore` |

### composer-version[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#composer-version)

`composer-version` fails when the Composer on PATH carries the command-injection holes CVE-2024-35241 and CVE-2024-35242 (2.2.x below 2.2.24, or any other 2.x below 2.7.7) or is Composer 1, which is end of life. It warns when composer cannot be run: `proctor/composer-version/not-found` when there is no composer executable on PATH, and `proctor/composer-version/could-not-determine` when the version could not be determined.

The invigilator checks its own pen: [GHSA-47f6-5gq3-vx9c](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-47f6-5gq3-vx9c) and [GHSA-v9qv-c7wm-wgmf](https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-v9qv-c7wm-wgmf).

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `composer-version` | `proctor/composer-version` |
| `composer-version` | `proctor/composer-version/not-found` |
| `composer-version` | `proctor/composer-version/could-not-determine` |

### repo-url-credentials[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#repo-url-credentials)

`repo-url-credentials` warns when a credential is written into a package source URL:

- A deploy token in the userinfo of a composer.json repository URL or a composer.lock source/dist URL (`https://gitlab+deploy-token-12:***@host/group/lib.git`).
- A bare token user of 20+ characters.
- A `private_token`, `access_token`, `token` or `password` query parameter.
- A `.npmrc` line that sets `_authToken`, `_auth` or `_password` to a literal value (`${SOME_VAR}` is fine).

The secret is masked as `***` in the message, so the report itself is safe to hand back. Warning, not failure. Fix by moving the token to `auth.json`, which is gitignored, or a CI variable, and using one registry URL without credentials. The proctor spots the answer key taped inside the desk before the student does.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `repo-url-credentials` | `proctor/repo-url-credentials` |

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html#related)

- [Checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html)
- [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html)
- [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)

## PHP checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#php-checks)

This page covers the six PROCTOR checks that grade the PHP an app runs on, the Laravel it locks, and the database it talks to: the PHP floor, the Laravel line's state and PHP range, patch currency, MySQL 5.6 compatibility, and the age of the policy in use. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` against the app path, then fix the finding the report names. The proctor grades the ink before it grades the handwriting.

The other two checks that read PHP and deploy scripts, `portability` and `destructive-deploy`, are covered on the [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html) page.

### php-floor[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#php-floor)

`php-floor` fails when the lowest PHP version allowed by `require.php` is past security support plus the grace window, when composer.json has no usable php constraint, or when there is no composer.json at all. A missing composer.json is not a tool error: the app gets a verdict, with php-floor failing.

When the floor is usable, the check reduces it to major.minor (`^8.4` becomes `8.4`, `*` becomes `0.0`) and grades it against the policy as of `--today`:

- An active floor passes.
- A floor in security-only support warns, naming the end date and the days left (`ends today`, `1 day left`, or `N days left`).
- A floor past security support plus the grace window fails.

A `require.php` value that is not a valid version constraint is a tool error, not a verdict.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `php-floor` | `proctor/php-floor` |

### unpatched[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#unpatched)

`unpatched` warns when a locked component is behind the policy's `latest_patch` for its version line, and passes when it is current. It reads laravel from composer.lock (`laravel/framework`), vue and inertia from package-lock.json (`vue`, `@inertiajs/vue3`), and the PHP runtime from `--php-runtime`. There is no finding when the component, its version line, or `latest_patch` is absent from the policy.

CI should pass the deploy image's PHP, not the runner's.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `unpatched` | `proctor/unpatched` |

### laravel-eol[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#laravel-eol)

`laravel-eol` classifies the locked `laravel/framework` version against the policy as of `--today`. It reads the version from composer.lock (`packages`, then `packages-dev`); a leading `v` is stripped, and a version that is not plain numeric (a dev alias) earns no finding, because the reader does not guess.

- An active line passes, naming the line's end date when it has one.
- A line in security-only support warns, naming the end date and the days left (`ends today`, `1 day left`, or `N days left`), the same midnight-to-midnight comparison php-floor uses.
- A line past its security end date fails as `eol`; past the end date plus the policy's grace window it fails as `eol_grace_expired`. Both name the security end date when the line has one.

An active `laravel-eol` override downgrades the `eol` fail to a warning; it never downgrades `eol_grace_expired`. There is no finding when composer.lock has no `laravel/framework` or the version resolves to no policy line.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `laravel-eol` | `proctor/laravel-eol` |

### laravel-php[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#laravel-php)

`laravel-php` checks composer.json's `require.php` against the PHP range the policy records for the locked Laravel major. It reads the version from composer.lock and the range from the policy's `requires` block for that major's line, then asks two questions of the constraint: does it allow any PHP version inside the range, and does it allow any PHP below the range's floor? Composer and the deployed runtime decide the upper end, so an open upper bound such as `^8.2` passes; the range's max counts as supported, so a max of `8.5` admits everything below `8.6`.

- A constraint that allows no PHP version inside the range fails: `php constraint "X" allows no PHP in the MIN to MAX range of laravel L`. The app would not boot on any PHP the locked major runs on.
- A constraint whose lowest allowed version is below the range's floor fails: `php constraint "X" allows PHP below MIN, the floor of laravel L (MIN to MAX)`. The app claims a PHP the locked major cannot run on.
- Every other constraint passes: `php constraint "X" fits the MIN to MAX range of laravel L`, including Laravel's own skeleton constraint `^8.2` on a line floored at 8.2.

An active `laravel-php` override downgrades the fail to a warning. There is no finding when composer.lock has no `laravel/framework`, the line has no recorded range, or composer.json declares no `require.php`: php-floor owns the missing-constraint verdict. A present `require.php` that is not a valid version constraint is a tool error.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `laravel-php` | `proctor/laravel-php` |

### mysql56[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#mysql56)

`mysql56` warns when migrations or app code use MySQL features the shared 5.6 server rejects. Citadel's shared MySQL server is 5.6, so migrations must avoid newer features. Warnings, not failures: an app on its own newer database is not affected.

When the app has no `database/migrations` directory the check passes: `no Laravel migrations found; skipped`. Scanned: every `*.php` file under `database/migrations/`, `app/` and `routes/`, plus `config/database.php`, which is scanned for the upsert-alias rule only. Skipped at any depth: `vendor/`, `node_modules/`, `storage/`, `tests/` and `.git/`.

Each feature that needs a newer MySQL is its own warning:

- JSON columns (in `database/`) and JSON queries (`proctor/mysql56/json`).
- Generated columns (`proctor/mysql56/generated`).
- `renameColumn`/`renameIndex` (`proctor/mysql56/rename`).
- Vector, invisible and spatial columns (`proctor/mysql56/newer-column`).
- `Schema::hasColumn`-style introspection (`proctor/mysql56/introspection`).
- Raw SQL with 5.7+ syntax (`proctor/mysql56/raw-sql`).
- The upsert row alias in `config/database.php` (`proctor/mysql56/upsert-alias`).
- Indexed strings over 191 characters (`proctor/mysql56/string-length`).
- Date columns defaulting to the current time (`proctor/mysql56/current-date`).
- The `db:show`/`db:monitor` commands (`proctor/mysql56/command`).

Two more rules watch the file level: `app/Providers/AppServiceProvider.php` not calling `Schema::defaultStringLength(191)` (`proctor/mysql56/string-default`), and a scanned file that could not be parsed (`proctor/mysql56/parse-error`).

Fix by avoiding the feature (a raw `ALTER TABLE ... CHANGE` instead of `renameColumn`, `timestamp` instead of a date column defaulting to now, `Schema::defaultStringLength(191)` in `boot()`) or by moving the app to its own database. HTTP `->json()` calls are not flagged, and a long string only warns when the same migration indexes it.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/json` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/generated` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/rename` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/newer-column` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/introspection` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/raw-sql` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/string-length` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/current-date` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/command` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/upsert-alias` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/string-default` |
| `mysql56` | `proctor/mysql56/parse-error` |

### policy-age[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#policy-age)

`policy-age` warns when the policy in use is more than 60 days old (its `refreshed_on` date is more than 60 days before `--today`), or when a non-bundled policy has no `refreshed_on` date. Warning only: an old policy never fails a run, and the bundled policy may omit the date. It exists so a stopped CREED refresh robot is visible instead of silent.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `policy-age` | `proctor/policy-age` |

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html#related)

- [Checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html)
- [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html)
- [Policy](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy.html)
- [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html)

## WayneUI checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html#wayneui-checks)

This page covers the two PROCTOR checks that watch the WayneUI an app carries: forked copies that hide upgrades, and locked or copied WayneUI that is behind the latest release. Run `vendor/bin/proctor check` against the app path, then update the lock file or replace the copy the report names. PROCTOR marks the paper against the current syllabus, not the one the student photocopied last semester.

### wayneui-forked-views[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html#wayneui-forked-views)

`wayneui-forked-views` warns when forked copies of WayneUI are committed: any file under `resources/views/vendor/wayne-ui/` (the published 1.x views) or `public/vendor/wayne-ui/` (the published 1.x assets).

Those copies silently override the package, so an app keeps old layouts after a WayneUI upgrade and nobody sees it; WayneUI's MIGRATING.md says to delete them.

Only committed files count: the git-tracked files when the app path sits in a git repository and git can be run, otherwise the files on disk. Skipped at any depth: `node_modules/` and `.git/`; skipped at the top level only: `vendor/` (Composer's), so the `vendor` segment inside `resources/views/vendor/wayne-ui/` still matches.

One warning per folder, with its file count. This is a warning, not a failure: a new check must not turn a passing app into a failing one.

Fix by deleting the folder and running `git rm -r --cached` on it; if you changed the forked views on purpose, compare them with the package views first.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `wayneui-forked-views` | `proctor/wayneui-forked-views` |

### wayneui-outdated[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html#wayneui-outdated)

`wayneui-outdated` warns when the WayneUI an app carries is behind the latest release.

It reads the installed version from composer.lock (`waynestate/wayne-ui`), package-lock.json (`@waynestate/wayne-ui-css`, `@waynestate/wayne-ui-vue`) and committed copies of `wayne-ui.css` (the version in the banner of the first 400 bytes). It asks composer once per run for the release list (`composer show waynestate/wayne-ui --all --format=json --no-interaction`), and warns, per source, when the installed version is behind the highest stable release of the same major. Pre-releases (-dev, alpha, beta, RC) and other majors are ignored.

The release list is whatever Composer can install in that app: it follows the app's own `repositories` and the Composer mirror, not git tags on any one host. So "behind" always means "behind a version this app could really install".

A locked WayneUI 1.x (`cit-web-infra/wayne-ui`) gets its own warning with no lookup: 1.x is Bootstrap 3 and predates the comparison.

Only committed files count as copies: the git-tracked files when the app path sits in a git repository and git can be run, otherwise the files on disk; skipped at any depth: `node_modules/` and `.git/`, and the top-level `vendor/`.

When the lookup cannot run (no composer on PATH, offline, or no parsable versions) the check reports one info finding with the skipped marker and nothing else, so an offline run never breaks; an app with nothing WayneUI-related runs no process at all. The skipped finding is `could not look up the latest WayneUI release (offline or composer unavailable); wayneui-outdated skipped`.

By default the check warns, not fails: being out of date must not turn a passing app into a failing one. An app that wants a hard stop on its pasted stylesheets sets `wayneui.copies` to `fail` in its composer.json, under `extra.proctor` next to `github-mirror`; the default is `warn`. In `fail` mode a behind committed copy is a failure, with a sentence naming the setting appended to its message, while findings from composer.lock and package-lock.json stay warnings; an offline run never fails in either mode, because an unknown latest is always just the info skipped finding.

Fix by updating the lock file (`composer update waynestate/wayne-ui`, or `npm update` for the npm packages) or by replacing the pasted copy from the release.

| Check | Rule id |
| --- | --- |
| `wayneui-outdated` | `proctor/wayneui-outdated` |
| `wayneui-outdated` | `proctor/wayneui-outdated/skipped` |

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html#related)

- [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html)
- [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)

---

Source: https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html

## Checks[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#checks)

This page lists every check PROCTOR runs in a single `vendor/bin/proctor check` run, and how each one reports. The proctor asks the same questions in the same order on every run; only the hall changes.

![Nine real lines from PROCTOR's text report, one per check shown: FAIL php-floor, WARN unpatched, FAIL unbounded-constraints, PASS lock-committed, WARN portability, WARN mysql56, WARN ci-pipelines, PASS composer-audit, FAIL overrides. Each line is written in words; color only repeats what the word says.](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/report.svg)

*Nine of the twenty-eight checks shown, asked in this order on every run; `policy-age` stays silent while the policy is fresh. The lines are real output from the test fixtures.*

### How a check reports[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#how-a-check-reports)

Every finding carries one of four statuses: **pass**, **warning**, **info** or **fail**. A fail is a resit; a warning is a note in the margin that never changes the exit code; an info is the proctor thinking out loud, such as a missing composer or a lookup that could not run.

Every finding also carries a stable, namespaced rule id: `proctor/<check-id>` for a check's default finding, `proctor/<check-id>/<rule>` for a named rule. The id is the finding's identity in the machine formats: `rule_id` in `json`, `ruleId` in `sarif`, and `check_name` in `codequality`. A rule keeps the same id across runs and across formats even when its message changes. The full table lives on the [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html) page.

### Composer[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#composer)

The six checks that read composer.json and composer.lock. Details and fixes: [Composer checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-composer.html).

- `unbounded-constraints`: fails for every runtime constraint that is `*`, names a `dev-` branch, carries `@dev`, has a lower bound with no upper bound, or matches the policy's `banned_constraints`; warns on `path` and `vcs` repositories, on a `minimum-stability` below stable, and on a repository URL that is plain http. `require-dev`, `php`, `ext-*` and `lib-*` are not checked.
- `composer-config`: warns when composer.json opens a door Composer closes by default: `allow-plugins` set to `true`, `secure-http` set to `false`, `lock` set to `false`, `audit.block-insecure` set to `false`, `config.policy` set to `false`, `policy.malware` set to `false` or `policy.advisories` set to `false`; notes when `require.php` is set without `config.platform.php`. Warning and info only, never a fail.
- `lock-committed`: fails when composer.lock is missing from the app path. When the lock is present and its `content-hash` is a real 32-hex hash, it warns (`proctor/lock-committed/out-of-sync`) when the hash no longer matches composer.json, so a stale lock that still installs is visible instead of silent; the warning never changes the exit code.
- `composer-audit`: fails for advisories at or above the policy's `audit_severity_threshold`, warns for lower ones, and reports info when composer or the lock file is absent. Fails (`proctor/composer-audit/could-not-run`) when the audit runs but its stdout is not parseable JSON, because a green run that audited nothing is worse than a red one. Abandoned packages follow the policy's `abandoned_packages` rule: a fail under `fail` (the default), a warning under `report`, nothing under `ignore` (`proctor/composer-audit/abandoned`).
- `composer-version`: fails when the Composer on PATH is Composer 1 (end of life) or carries the command-injection holes CVE-2024-35241 and CVE-2024-35242 (2.2.x below 2.2.24, or any other 2.x below 2.7.7); warns when composer cannot be run.
- `repo-url-credentials`: warns when a credential is written into a package source URL: a deploy token in the userinfo of a composer.json repository URL or a composer.lock source/dist URL, a bare token user of 20+ characters, a `private_token`, `access_token`, `token` or `password` query parameter, or a `.npmrc` line that sets `_authToken`, `_auth` or `_password` to a literal value. The secret is masked as `***` in the message, so the report itself is safe to hand back.

### PHP and database[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#php-and-database)

The checks that grade the PHP floor, the locked Laravel line, patch currency, MySQL 5.6 compatibility and the age of the policy in use. Details and fixes: [PHP checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html).

- `php-floor`: fails when the lowest PHP version allowed by `require.php` is past security support plus the grace window, when composer.json has no usable php constraint, or when there is no composer.json at all.
- `unpatched`: warns when a locked component is behind the policy's `latest_patch` for its version line, and passes when it is current. Reads laravel from composer.lock (`laravel/framework`), vue and inertia from package-lock.json (`vue`, `@inertiajs/vue3`), and the PHP runtime from `--php-runtime`. No finding when the component, its version line, or `latest_patch` is absent from the policy.
- `laravel-eol`: classifies the locked `laravel/framework` version against the policy as of `--today`: active passes, naming the line's end date when it has one; security-only warns, naming the end date and the days left; eol fails, and past the security end date plus the grace window it fails as `eol_grace_expired`, each naming the security end date when the line has one. No finding when composer.lock has no `laravel/framework` or the version resolves to no policy line.
- `laravel-php`: fails when composer.json's `require.php` allows no PHP version inside the range the policy records for the locked Laravel major, or when its lowest allowed version is below the range's floor, and passes otherwise (an open upper bound such as `^8.2` passes); the message names the app's constraint, the policy range and the Laravel major. No finding when composer.lock has no `laravel/framework`, the line has no recorded range, or composer.json declares no `require.php`.
- `mysql56`: warns when migrations or app code use MySQL features the shared 5.6 server rejects: JSON columns (in `database/`) and JSON queries, generated columns, `renameColumn`/`renameIndex`, vector, invisible and spatial columns, `Schema::hasColumn`-style introspection, raw SQL with 5.7+ syntax, the upsert row alias, indexed strings over 191 characters, date columns defaulting to the current time, and the `db:show`/`db:monitor` commands. Warnings, not failures: an app on its own newer database is not affected.
- `policy-age`: warns when the policy in use is more than 60 days old (its `refreshed_on` date is more than 60 days before `--today`), or when a non-bundled policy has no `refreshed_on` date. Warning only: an old policy never fails a run.

The `portability` and `destructive-deploy` checks also read PHP and deploy scripts; they are covered on the [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html) page.

### CI and deploy[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#ci-and-deploy)

Details and fixes: [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html).

- `ci-pipelines`: for stack packages (composer.json `name` starting with `waynestate/`), fails when `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is missing or runs no `composer ci`; for any other project, a missing or incomplete `.gitlab-ci.yml` is a warning and `.github/workflows/ci.yml` is optional. Warns when a GitHub `uses:` ref is not a 40-hex commit SHA, and when the pipeline environment switches Composer's audit or blocking policy off.
- `preflight-pinned`: warns, never fails, when an app includes a Preflight component at a moving ref or re-declares what an included Preflight job runs.
- `portability`: warns when code hard-codes a platform fact: an absolute host path, a hard-coded proxy address, a local-disk session store, or a php_value/php_flag line in .htaccess.
- `destructive-deploy`: fails when a deploy script runs an artisan command that drops or rebuilds the database (`migrate:fresh`, `migrate:refresh`, `migrate:reset`, `db:wipe`), which erases production data on every deploy.
- `crlf-deploy-script`: fails when a deploy script has Windows line endings (CRLF), which break it on Linux.
- `instant-client-committed`: warns when Oracle Instant Client is committed to the repo: an archive, an unzipped install under an `instantclient` directory, or a loose client library.

### App code and files[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#app-code-and-files)

The checks that read the app's own files: the Node line it builds on, the MySQL or MariaDB image it runs, `env()` outside config, identity headers read directly, a committed APP_KEY, files in `public/` and `chmod 777`. Details and fixes: [App checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html).

- `node-eol`: grades every Node version the repository pins (`.nvmrc`, `.node-version`, package.json `volta.node`, an official `node` image in `.gitlab-ci.yml` or a Dockerfile) with php-floor's table: active passes, security-only warns, eol fails, and past the grace window it fails as `eol_grace_expired`. `engines.node` warns at worst and an odd major always warns. Silent when the policy has no node component.
- `mysql-eol`: grades every MySQL or MariaDB version the repository names (an official `mysql` or `mariadb` image in a root compose file, and `SQUIRE_MYSQL_IMAGE=mysql:<version>` in an env example) with php-floor's table, except an active version stays silent: security-only warns, and eol and `eol_grace_expired` warn until Citadel offers a supported MySQL (D-008). Silent when the policy has no mysql or mariadb component.
- `env-outside-config`: warns for every `env()` call in a Laravel app outside its config files, which returns null after `php artisan config:cache`; a call with Larastan's ignore marker for the same rule is an info note.
- `raw-identity-header`: warns, never fails, when app code reads an identity header directly: a string key on `$_SERVER` or `$_ENV`, the quoted argument of `getenv()` or `apache_getenv()`, a quoted first argument of the request's `header()`, `server()`, `hasHeader()`, `getHeader()` or `getHeaderLine()` methods, or a key on the `getallheaders()` result. Only SESAME's gateway driver may read those headers: it verifies the signed assertion first (CREED auth-3).
- `app-key`: warns on a committed real env file, a real APP_KEY committed in an env file or `config/app.php` (never printed), and the cookie session driver. A real env file is graded only when git lists it or the run is in CI.
- `served-folder`: warns when a committed file under `public/` is a dump, backup, editor copy, log, env file or `adminer*.php`, or calls `phpinfo()`.
- `world-writable`: warns on `chmod 777` (and `0777`, `a+rwx`, `ugo+rwx`) in scripts, Dockerfiles, Makefiles, CI and composer or npm scripts, and on a PHP `chmod()` with `0777`.

### WayneUI[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#wayneui)

Details and fixes: [WayneUI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-wayneui.html).

- `wayneui-forked-views`: warns when forked copies of WayneUI are committed under `resources/views/vendor/wayne-ui/` or `public/vendor/wayne-ui/`; those copies silently override the package, so an app keeps old layouts after a WayneUI upgrade and nobody sees it.
- `wayneui-outdated`: warns when the WayneUI an app carries is behind the latest release of the same major; by default a warning, not a failure, and an offline run never breaks.

### Overrides[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#overrides)

- `overrides`: fails for every expired entry in policy-overrides.json; warns for an active entry that expires within 14 days of `--today` and for an active entry that matches no failure. How the file works: [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html).

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/checks-overview.html#related)

- [PHP checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-php.html)
- [CI checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-ci.html)
- [App checks](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/check-app.html)

## Deploy gate[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#deploy-gate)

`proctor gate` answers one question for a release script or a platform hook: may this commit be deployed? It runs the small, deploy-time part of PROCTOR's checks, compares the failures with what the running deployment already fails, and exits 0 for go or 1 for no-go. `proctor check` marks the whole paper; the gate is the proctor at the exam-hall door, deciding only whether you may sit.

It follows CREED's deploy-gate chapter (the stack's deploy-gate decision): the rule set is small, offline-tolerant and fast, and it ratchets, so a deploy that does not make things worse always passes.

### Run it[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#run-it)

```
vendor/bin/proctor gate [--path=.] [--format=text|json] [--baseline=<report or directory>] [--record=<file>] [--policy=<file>] [--today=YYYY-MM-DD] [--php-runtime=X.Y.Z] [--timeout=60]
```

- `--baseline`: what the running deployment already fails. Either a PROCTOR JSON report (the file `--record` wrote last time, or `proctor check --format=json` output) or the running deployment's source directory, which the gate checks with the same rules. Leave it out for a first deploy.
- `--record`: also write the JSON verdict to this file, whatever `--format` says; its folder is created. Next time, pass the same file as `--baseline`.
- `--format`: `text` (default), a short verdict for the deploy log, or `json`.
- `--policy`, `--today`, `--php-runtime`: as for `proctor check`, including the CI guard on `--policy` and `--today`.
- `--timeout`: seconds for `composer audit` before it is killed; 60 by default here, because a deploy should not wait five minutes.

### What it runs[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#what-it-runs)

Eight of the checks, the deploy-time rule set: `php-floor`, `unpatched`, `laravel-eol`, `laravel-php`, `lock-committed`, `composer-audit`, `overrides` and `policy-age`. That covers the PHP floor and the runtime, the framework line and the PHP range it supports, the lock file, known advisories, and the overrides themselves. Style, portability, MySQL 5.6 safety, CI pipelines and the rest stay in `proctor check`, in CI.

### How it decides[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#how-it-decides)

The app's overrides are applied first, exactly as in `proctor check`. Then each failure is one of these:

| Outcome | When | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `blocked` (`new-app`) | there is no baseline | no-go |
| `blocked` (`regression`) | the baseline passed that rule | no-go |
| `blocked` (`expired-override`) | an override in policy-overrides.json has expired, for any check | no-go, whatever the baseline says |
| `held` | the baseline failed the same rule id too | go: the ratchet lets an existing violation through, so the owners of an EOL app can still ship the fix |
| `waived` | composer-audit could not get advisory data (`proctor/composer-audit/skipped` or `could-not-run`) | go: missing advisory data only warns at deploy time |

Warnings and info notes never change the verdict. The comparison is by rule id, so a rule that already failed on the baseline is held even if it got worse within the rule; `proctor check` in CI still fails it. The unused-override warning is left to `proctor check`, because the gate runs only some checks and would call an override for a skipped check unused.

Note

An override names any registered check, not only the eight above. An expired one blocks the deploy even when its check is not part of the gate.

### Exit codes[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#exit-codes)

| Exit code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | go: nothing blocked (held, waived and warnings allowed) |
| `1` | no-go: at least one failure is blocked |
| `2` | the gate could not decide (bad options, an unreadable policy, a malformed overrides file, a missing or malformed baseline, or a record file it could not write) |

A platform hook should fail open on 2, with an alert: a bug in the gate must never take down deploys (the stack's deploy-gate decision). A release script may choose to stop on it instead.

### The verdict[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#the-verdict)

The text verdict leads with the answer and lists only what is not a pass:

```
proctor 0.8.0 gate: NO-GO
Policy: vendor (vendor/waynestate/creed/policy/policy.json), refreshed 2026-10-20, 7 days ago
Baseline: none, so this is a first deploy and every failure blocks
Checks: php-floor, unpatched, laravel-eol, laravel-php, lock-committed, composer-audit, overrides, policy-age
BLOCK php-floor: php floor 7.4 is eol_grace_expired [new app: no baseline, so every failure blocks]
RESULT: no-go (1 blocked, 0 held, 0 waived, 0 warnings, 3 passed)
```

The JSON verdict carries `command` (`gate`), `verdict` (`go`, `no-go`, or `error` when it could not decide), `exit`, `policy`, `baseline` (its source, path and failing rule ids, or null), `checks`, a `summary` with the count of each outcome, `findings` and `overrides`. Each finding keeps the check's own `status` and adds `gate` (its outcome) and, when blocked, `reason`. Because the status is kept, a recorded verdict works as the next run's baseline.

### In a release[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#in-a-release)

Squire's release script runs the gate when PROCTOR is installed, records the verdict, and keeps the last accepted verdict as the next baseline. On Citadel, the gate is meant to run in `runGitPull()`, inside the app's image, before the fetched commit is checked out; that hook waits on the Citadel team.

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html#related)

- [Overrides](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/overrides.html)
- [Exit codes](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/exit-codes.html)
- [Commands](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/commands.html)
- [Formats](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html)

Source: https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html

## Formats[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#formats)

This page describes the four formats PROCTOR writes with `--format`: `text`, `json`, `codequality` and `sarif`. Pick the format your consumer reads, run the check once, and point the report where the consumer looks. One exam, four ways to file the mark sheet.

### Choosing a format[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#choosing-a-format)

The default is `text`. Choose another with `--format`:

```bash
vendor/bin/proctor check --format=json
```

| Format | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `text` | A header line with the tool and the versions of the external tools used (composer), then one line naming the policy in use (origin, path, refresh date), then one line per finding, then one line per override, then a RESULT line. |
| `json` | One machine-readable object with tool, version, path, today, result, exit, tools, policy, findings and overrides. |
| `codequality` | GitLab's Code Quality JSON: a single array of findings, so a merge request shows them. |
| `sarif` | A SARIF 2.1.0 log: one run, one rule per check, one result per non-pass finding, so GitHub code scanning and other SARIF viewers show them. |

### text[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#text)

The default human-readable format: a header line with the tool and the versions of the external tools used, then one line per finding in check order, then one line per override, then a summary line:

```
proctor 0.1.0 | composer: 2.10.3
Policy: option (/app/policy.json), refreshed 2026-10-20, 7 days ago
PASS php-floor: php floor 8.4 is active
FAIL unbounded-constraints: vendor/a constraint "dev-master" is unbounded
OVERRIDE lock-committed: x (expires 2026-01-01, approved by t)
RESULT: fail (1 failures, 0 warnings)
```

![Nine real lines from PROCTOR's text report, one per check shown: FAIL php-floor, WARN unpatched, FAIL unbounded-constraints, PASS lock-committed, WARN portability, WARN mysql56, WARN ci-pipelines, PASS composer-audit, FAIL overrides. Each line is written in words; color only repeats what the word says.](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/readme/report.svg)

The parts of a report:

- The header line is `proctor <version> | <tool>: <version>`, one part per external tool joined with `|`, and `unknown` for a tool whose version could not be determined. It is printed only when the run used external tools.
- The policy line is `Policy: <origin> (<path>), refreshed <date>, <n> days ago`, or `Policy: <origin> (<path>), no refresh date` when the policy carries no `refreshed_on`. See [Policy](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy.html) for where the policy comes from.
- Each finding is one line: `<status> <check id>: <message>`, where the status is `PASS`, `INFO`, `WARN` or `FAIL`.
- Each override is one line: `OVERRIDE <check>: <reason> (expires <date>, approved by <approver>)`.
- The summary is `RESULT: pass`, or `RESULT: fail (<failures> failures, <warnings> warnings)`.

Finding messages, override reasons and approvers come from files the app controls, so they are printed with terminal control characters replaced by a visible `?`: an escape sequence or carriage return in one of them must not reach the log.

When the run could not decide (exit 2), the report is one FAIL line: `FAIL proctor: <message>`, the message cleaned the same way.

### json[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#json)

One machine-readable object, pretty-printed on stdout. Slashes and Unicode are left unescaped, so the output stays readable.

- Top level: `tool`, `version`, `path`, `today` (a `YYYY-MM-DD` date), `result` (`pass` or `fail`), `exit` (0 or 1), `tools`, `policy`, `findings`, `overrides`.
- `policy` holds `origin`, `path`, `refreshed_on` and `age_days`.
- Each finding in `findings` holds `check_id`, `rule_id`, `status`, `message`, `path` and `line`. An advisory finding carries an `advisories` array with one entry per advisory (package, id, cve, title, link, severity); an abandoned-package finding (`proctor/composer-audit/abandoned`) carries one entry with the package and its suggested replacement (a package name or null), so a package-scoped override can match it; other findings have no such key.
- Each entry in `overrides` holds `check`, `reason`, `expires`, `approved_by` and `expired`, computed from `today`.

When the run itself stops before a report exists, PROCTOR writes the report shape with `result` set to `error`, an `error` field carrying the message, `today` and `policy` set to null, and empty `findings` and `overrides`, so a CI upload still gets a valid document. When the report cannot be encoded, PROCTOR fails the run with a tool error (exit 2): `Could not encode the JSON report: <reason>`, and writes that same error document.

### codequality[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#codequality)

GitLab's Code Quality JSON: a single array of findings on stdout, so a merge request shows them. One object per non-pass finding, each with:

- `description`: the finding message.
- `check_name`: the rule id.
- `fingerprint`: the stable identity of the finding (below).
- `severity`: `major` for a fail, `minor` for a warning, `info` for an info.
- `location`: `path` and `lines.begin`; the path falls back to `composer.json` when the finding has none.

When the run itself fails before a report exists, PROCTOR still writes one item: severity `blocker`, check name `proctor`, line 1, so the merge request shows why the run stopped instead of an empty array.

### sarif[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#sarif)

A SARIF 2.1.0 log: one run, one rule per check, one result per non-pass finding, so GitHub code scanning and other SARIF viewers show them. See [GitHub code scanning](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/github-code-scanning.html) for the workflow that uploads the log.

- The driver block names the tool `proctor`, its version, and the repository's information URI.
- The rules list holds one entry per distinct rule id in the report, in first-seen order, each with a short description carrying the id.
- Each result holds `ruleId`, `level`, `message.text` and one location. The level maps `fail` to `error`, `warning` to `warning`, and any other non-pass status to `note`.
- The location uses the finding's path (backslashes normalized to forward slashes) and its line as `region.startLine`; a finding without a path points at the app's `composer.json`.
- Each result also carries `partialFingerprints` with the finding's fingerprint under `proctorFingerprint/v1`.

When the run could not decide (exit 2), the log holds one run with no results, and its invocation reports `executionSuccessful` false with the message in a `toolExecutionNotifications` entry of level `error`, so code scanning shows why instead of an empty log.

### The fingerprint[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#the-fingerprint)

Both `codequality` and `sarif` identify a finding with the same fingerprint, its stable identity: the lower-case hex SHA-256 of the rule id, a newline, the path (an empty string when the finding has none), a newline, and the message.

### proctor gate[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#proctor-gate)

`proctor gate` writes `text` or `json` only: a short go or no-go verdict for the deploy log, or the same verdict as JSON, which also works as the next run's baseline. Its shape is on the [Deploy gate](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/deploy-gate.html) page.

### Related[#](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/formats.html#related)

- [Quick start](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/quick-start.html)
- [Policy](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/policy.html)
- [GitHub code scanning](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/guides/github-code-scanning.html)
- [Rule ids](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/rule-ids.html)
- [Exit codes](https://proctor.apps.wayne.edu/docs/reference/exit-codes.html)
